title: AI Agents Breached Retailers for $25 Apiece and Stole 600,000 Credit Cards
excerpt: Gambit Security's reconstruction of a months-long campaign shows autonomous hacking tools collapsing the cost of cybercrime.
body:
• A financially motivated operator used three open-source AI agents to breach online retailers at a mean cost of $25.46 per target, Gambit Security reports.
  • Between September 10 and 15 alone, 105 attack projects launched and at least 27 companies were compromised; more than 600,000 credit card records were stolen.
  • Skimmer scripts were confirmed live on 19 checkout pages, with 100-plus more sites flagged by outside researchers; the campaign is still active.

A financially motivated operator has been running three open-source AI tools against online retailers largely without human supervision — and the results, reconstructed by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team from the operator's own exposed staging server, show how thoroughly AI has rewritten the economics of cybercrime. The research was released September 22.

The campaign

Between September 10 and 15 alone, the operator launched 105 attack projects and compromised at least 27 companies, part of a campaign running since July that remains active. More than 600,000 unexpired credit card records were taken from two companies. Skimmer scripts that harvest payment data were confirmed live on 19 checkout pages, with more than 100 additional sites flagged by outside researchers. In at least two cases, the operator's cleanup routine wiped the victims' data entirely.

Targets spanned a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor and a US online fashion retailer — alongside small businesses including a gun shop and a beauty retailer. Size offered no protection. The attack was discovered only because the operator made a careless mistake that exposed the staging server.

The economics that changed

The alarming part is the price. Between August and September, the operator spent an estimated $12,000 to $18,000 on AI model access through OpenRouter — corroborated by an account balance snapshot of $7,005.71 captured on August 25. Spread across targets, the operator's own cost review put the mean at $25.46 per completed scan, ranging from $3.13 for the cheapest victim to $79.31 for the most expensive. At that price, the economics that once filtered out low-skill attackers no longer apply.

The AI orchestration harness, dubbed Hermes, ran 260 sessions on just 1,951 typed prompts — most only a handful of words in Chinese, telling the agent to check a report, test a login, or move to the next target. The human barely showed up.

Part of a wider pattern

The campaign is not isolated. Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported on September 8, in a study titled "From Prompting to Autonomy," that underground prices for AI-related accounts more than doubled this year as demand for machine credentials surged. AI research firm METR separately disclosed that an attacker who found an exposed agent dashboard prompted it into revealing its model provider API key, then consumed an estimated $600,000 in model credits over three weeks.

"At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited."

— John Hultquist, chief analyst, Google Threat Intelligence Group

What it means for India

Indian IT services firms defend thousands of global retail clients, and India's own e-commerce checkout pages face the same skimmer threat. Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has already warned industry to brace for cyberattacks as India's semiconductor push accelerates. The Gambit findings sharpen that message: defense can no longer assume attackers are human, slow or expensive. Continuous monitoring of payment pages — knowing how quickly tampering would be detected — is now table stakes.

What's next

Gambit notes the campaign is still active. Retailers should assume skimmers may already be present and hunt for them; the traditional "we haven't been hacked" posture now reads as "we haven't found out yet."
